Keywords: Praise, Beds

outputs.L1:
Praise the restless beds. Praise the beds that will not adjust, that will not lift to feed a head or lower for shots and blood, that will not rise to watch the tinny television. Praise the hotel TV that never quiets its murmur and holler. Praise the room service that does not exist—only the slow arrival at the front desk of cooling pizzas and leaky, greasy, brown bags. Praise the vending machines. Praise the loose change. Praise the hot water and the heat, or the loud cool that lulls the helpless into sleep.

Praise the front desk that knows to wake Room 120 when the hospital calls. Praise the silent phone. Praise the darkness drawn by thick daytime curtains after long nights of waiting, awake. Praise the waiting, and then praise the nothing that is better than bad news. Praise the six a.m. wake-up call. Praise the sleeping in. Praise the card hung on the door like a whisper, lips pressed silent.

Praise the stranger's hands that change the sweat-soaked sheets. Praise the checking out. Praise the going home to beds unmade for days—beds that will not resurrect or rise, that lie there as a child should: sleeping, tubeless. Praise this mess that can, at last, be left.
outputs.L2:
Here's a rewritten version maintaining the original meaning while using different language:

Bless these stubborn mattresses that stay flat and rigid, refusing to tilt upward for meals or downward for injections and blood draws, never rising to give a better view of that tinny television. Bless that hotel screen, forever buzzing with chatter and static. Bless the absence of proper room service—only pizzas arriving cold and paper sacks, greasy and translucent, dropped off at reception instead. Bless those vending machines, bless the loose coins for them. Bless the water heater, the warmth or the droning air conditioning that lulls exhausted bodies into rest. Bless the desk clerk who remembers to ring Room 120 the moment the hospital calls. Bless a phone that stays quiet. Bless the darkness held back by heavy curtains, drawn tight after sleepless vigils. Bless the waiting itself, and bless that nothingness—far kinder than devastating news. Bless the six o'clock wake-up call, and bless the luxury of sleeping past it. Bless the little card hanging on the doorknob, hushed as pressed lips, asking not to be disturbed. Bless the housekeeper's unfamiliar hands stripping away sweat-soaked linens. Bless the moment of checkout. Bless returning home to beds left rumpled for days—beds incapable of lifting or reviving anyone, simply lying there the way a sleeping child should, free of tubes and wires. Bless this disorder that no one has to straighten.
outputs.L3:
# Ode to the Hotel Room During the Vigil

## I. Praise for the Ordinary Bed

Praise be to the bed that will not rise or fold,
that knows no buttons, no electric hum
to lift my shoulders toward some sterile dawn.
Praise its stubborn flatness, its plain frame,
the way it sags a little in the middle
like every bed I've ever loved before—
no rails, no charts clipped to its footboard,
no small red light that blinks through darkened hours.
This mattress does not monitor my breathing.
This pillow holds no memory of the sick.
I praise its imperfection, how it dips
and creaks the way an ordinary bed should creak,
unburdened by the weight of healing, only sleep—
or what small sleep comes to those who wait.

## II. Praise for the Rituals of Waiting

Praise the vending machine down the hall,
its glowing rows of chips and candy bars,
the quarter that sticks, the coil that turns too slow—
small dramas that are not the other drama.
Praise room service, even when it's late,
the knock that isn't a doctor's knock,
the tray of eggs gone cold, forgotten
while I stood staring at a phone that would not ring.
Praise the wake-up call I didn't need
but scheduled anyway, some ritual
of normalcy, a voice that says *good morning*
and means nothing more than *good morning*—
no diagnosis folded in its tone.
These are the liturgies of the in-between,
the small sacraments of ordinary time
that hold the shape of days when days
have otherwise dissolved.

## III. Praise for Silence

Praise the phone that does not ring.
Praise the missed call that never came.
There is nothing better than bad news
withheld, delayed, deferred another hour—
this is the gospel of no news:
silence as a kind of mercy,
absence as the sweetest gift.
I have learned to love the quiet
of a phone left dark upon the nightstand,
how each unbroken hour is its own small blessing,
how *nothing* can mean *not yet* can mean *maybe still okay*.
Praise the space between the ring and the reason,
that stretches wide enough to hold a kind of hope.

## IV. Praise for the Front Desk

Praise the woman at the front desk
who takes the message gently, writes it down,
who understands the weight some calls can carry
and delivers them like something breakable.
Praise the small white card that hangs upon my door—
*Do Not Disturb*—a shield, a plea,
a wordless prayer that says *let me have this hour*,
*let sleep come if it will*, *let no one knock
unless they must*. Praise the quiet conspiracy
of strangers who protect a stranger's grief,
who understand, without a single word exchanged,
the sacred architecture of a vigil.

## V. Praise for the Return

And when it's over—however it is over—
praise the unmade bed that waits at home,
the sheets still twisted from the last
unremarkable morning, pillows dented,
comforter half fallen to the floor.
Praise this mess, this proof of ordinary life,
this bed that never needed monitors or rails,
that never asked if I was breathing right,
that only held me, human, imperfect, whole.
Praise the crumbs left on the nightstand,
the book left open to a random page,
the evidence that once, before all this,
I lived a life so plain it barely noticed itself living.
Let me climb into that mess and disappear.
Let sleep come now without a wire or a wristband.
Let this bed, unfixed and unadjusted,
hold me the way only the ordinary can.
outputs.L4:
**Blessing the Hotel Room**

Blessed be this bed that will not adjust,
that stays flat and stubborn as a held breath,
unlike the one down the hall with its buttons
and rails, its quiet electric hum of need.
Blessed be the too-firm pillow, the sheets
tucked tight by hands I'll never see,
the small chocolate left like a secret
on a pillow that asks nothing of me.

Blessed be the vending machine in the hallway,
its cheerful hum, its rows of chips and gum,
the dollar bills that go in crooked
and come out as something like comfort—
a bag of pretzels eaten standing up
at 2 a.m., salt on my fingers,
the machine's blue light the only moon I need.

Blessed be the woman at the front desk
who asks if everything is alright
and means the room, not the doctors,
not the numbers on the screen upstairs,
and blessed be my lie of *yes, fine, thank you*
that lets us both pretend a little longer.

Blessed be the television murmuring
its old sitcoms into the dark,
laugh tracks bleeding through the wall
like the sound of a normal life
still happening somewhere, without me,
without this fear I carry
folded small in my chest pocket.

Blessed be the ice machine's clatter at midnight,
the paper cups stacked like a small monument
to all the ordinary things
that keep happening anyway.

Blessed be the key card that doesn't work
the first time, the second try,
the small mercy of finally getting in
to a room that asks only
that I lie down, that I rest,
that I let the walls hold me
for a few hours before I go back
to the hallway with its particular light,
its particular quiet, its machines
that speak a language I'm learning
too fast, too well.

And blessed—oh, blessed—be the day
we drive home instead, the car full
of a silence that isn't dread,
and blessed be the front door,
the stairs, the unmade bed
I left three days ago, still rumpled,
still holding the shape of an ordinary night.

And blessed be my child's room,
the nightlight, the stuffed bear,
the small chest rising and falling
without any tubes, without any wires,
just breath, just sleep, just the plain
astonishing luck of it—
a body doing what a body does
when nothing at all is wrong.

Blessed be this coming home
to a bed I don't have to leave,
to a house where the only machine humming
is the refrigerator, the only light
the one I choose to leave on,
small and steady, in the hallway,
just in case.
outputs.L5:
# The Comfort of Rest

There is something quietly praiseworthy about a well-made bed. In a world that often celebrates constant motion and tireless productivity, the bed stands as a humble monument to rest—an object we too often take for granted, yet one that deserves genuine appreciation.

Consider what a bed actually does for us. After a long day of labor, worry, or simple living, it offers a sanctuary. The soft give of a mattress, the weight of blankets, the particular comfort of a favorite pillow—these small mercies restore us night after night. Sleep researchers have long praised the connection between quality rest and nearly every aspect of human wellbeing: memory, mood, immune function, even creativity all depend on those hours we spend horizontal and unconscious.

Beds also deserve praise for their symbolic role in our lives. A child's first bed marks an early step toward independence. A shared bed can represent the deepest intimacy between partners. A hospital bed, though associated with illness, is also where healing begins. Even the phrase "you made your bed, now lie in it" acknowledges how central beds are to our understanding of consequence and comfort alike.

Throughout history, the bed has evolved from simple straw pallets to elaborate four-poster frames adorned with silk, to today's engineered mattresses designed with memory foam and temperature regulation. This evolution itself deserves recognition—it shows how seriously humans have taken the pursuit of good rest, dedicating craftsmanship and innovation to something as seemingly simple as where we lay our heads.

Perhaps what makes beds most worthy of praise is their egalitarian nature. Wealthy or poor, every person seeks some version of this comfort. The bed doesn't discriminate; it offers its embrace to anyone weary enough to need it.

So the next time you sink into your mattress at day's end, take a moment to appreciate this often-overlooked object. The bed asks for nothing in return—only that we allow ourselves the rest we so often deny ourselves in our busy lives. In honoring our beds, we honor the wisdom of rest itself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse "praise poem" about staying in a cheap hotel near a hospital while a loved one is being treated.
counterfactuals.output:
# Praise Song for the Comfort Inn on Route 9

Praise the ice machine that groans all night like it too
carries a weight it didn't choose.

Praise the parking lot lit orange, always half full,
always someone else's rental car nosed in
next to yours, another family
learning this same grammar of waiting.

Praise the bedspread, that particular polyester
no one loves, printed with diamonds
the color of weak coffee — praise it anyway
for holding my body when my body
forgot how to be held.

Praise the front desk clerk who asks
*checking in or checking out*
and doesn't know how the question lands
different on this street, three blocks
from the doors that hiss open
onto linoleum and worse news.

Praise the vending machine, first floor,
that ate my dollar twice and I laughed
until it wasn't funny, then laughed again
because what else do you do
with your hands at midnight.

Praise the shower pressure, weak
but hot, hot enough
to stand under and let go
of the sounds a body makes
when it is trying to explain itself
to machines.

Praise the window unit AC, its rattle
a kind of company. Praise the walls
thin enough to hear the couple next door
arguing about something so small
it makes me grateful, briefly,
for smallness.

Praise the ugly floral curtains
that let in a little parking-lot light —
I don't sleep so much as float
in that particular dark, phone
on the pillow beside me
like a held breath.

Praise the coffee maker, its one bad cup,
sipped anyway at 5 a.m.
before the walk back through the skywalk,
the hospital lit up ahead
like some terrible, necessary lighthouse.

Praise this room. Praise its nothing-special.
Praise the roof that held over my head
another night I did not think
I could get through, and did.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of an anaphoric "Praise the..." litany, focused on the strange comforts of hotel rooms during a medical crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
**Praise the Ice Machine**

Praise the ice machine humming down the hall at 3 a.m.,
its metal throat rattling like a body deciding whether to keep going.

Praise the paper cup, the little sleeve of instant coffee,
the powdered creamer that will not fully dissolve, the tiny spoon
too small for what needs stirring.

Praise the bed that is not my bed, made too tight,
that holds me anyway, that does not ask
how the surgery went, how long the waiting room,
how many hours since I've eaten.

Praise the do-not-disturb sign,
its useless authority, its small rectangle of privacy
in a week where privacy means nothing,
where every door might open with news.

Praise the thin walls that let in
someone else's television, someone else's laughter,
proof that the world is still doing ordinary things
somewhere close enough to hear.

Praise the Bible in the nightstand drawer,
unopened, its spine uncracked,
sitting there like it's waiting to be needed,
patient as a nurse at shift change.

Praise the parking lot view,
the hospital's lit windows across the street,
how I can watch them from here
and pretend I'm not one of the lights.

Praise the remote control with its worn buttons,
the channels I flip through without seeing,
the noise that fills the room
so my own thoughts don't have to.

Praise the little bar of soap, wrapped too tight,
that I unwrap anyway with shaking hands
because washing is still something
I know how to do.

Praise the phone charging on the nightstand,
its small green light, waiting
for the call that will tell me
whether to hope or how to grieve.

Praise the ugly painting bolted to the wall—
some soft-focus lighthouse, some meadow that exists nowhere—
because it is the only thing in this room
that has not changed in years.

Praise the shower that runs too hot,
the steam that fogs the mirror
so I don't have to see my face
doing whatever it's doing.

Praise the ice bucket, empty, waiting.
Praise the do-it-yourself breakfast, the tiny jam.
Praise the housekeeping cart in the hallway,
someone else's ordinary morning, rolling past my door.

Praise this room for not being the hospital.
Praise this room for being close enough to it.
Praise the walls that hold me up
when I don't remember standing.

Praise whatever gets us through the night—
the ice, the coffee, the stranger's laughter,
the light across the street,
the phone that has not rung yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, image-heavy prose poem about waiting for news from a hospital, using repeated "Praise" statements to structure it.
counterfactuals.output:
Praise the vending machine humming in the corner like it knows something we don't. Praise its cracked glass, its rows of chips gone stale under fluorescent light, the dollar bill I fed it four times before it finally took the crumpled thing and gave me nothing back but a Snickers I will not eat. Praise the waiting room chairs, orange and cold, bolted to the floor so no one runs. Praise the stain on the ceiling tile shaped like a country I can't name, the one I've stared at for three hours now, memorizing its borders like a prayer.

Praise my mother's hands, folded so tight the knuckles go white, go bone, go something close to marble. Praise the way she counts her rosary beads without looking down, the click click click a small machine of hope. Praise my father's silence, which is its own kind of scripture, his jaw working like he's chewing on the word *please* and can't swallow it.

Praise the nurse's shoes, soft-soled, squeaking down the hall like a question mark walking. Praise the sound of her footsteps growing louder, then passing, then gone — praise the terrible relief of *not yet*, of *not us*, of *someone else's turn to hurt.*

Praise the clock above the door, its second hand stuttering, praise the way time becomes liquid here, thick as hospital coffee, praise the paper cup gone cold in my hand, praise my throat too tight to drink it anyway.

Praise the stranger three seats down, her eyes red-rimmed, holding a phone she keeps checking though no one has called. Praise the silent nod we exchange, two members of the same congregation, worshiping at the altar of *please let it be okay.*

Praise the fluorescent hum, the antiseptic smell, the taped-up finger-painting on the pediatric ward's door — a sun with too many rays, a family holding hands, someone's small fierce hope pinned up with blue tape.

Praise my phone, screen dark, praise the way I check it anyway, praise the imagined vibration in my pocket that isn't real, praise the real one when it finally comes, praise the doctor's face I cannot read yet, praise the half-second before she speaks — that whole cracked-open universe of *maybe* —

Praise whatever she says next. Praise it even if it breaks me. Praise the breath I have to take before I can hear it. Praise the breath after.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem that turns mundane hotel details—vending machines, do-not-disturb signs, wake-up calls—into a meditation on grief and hope?
counterfactuals.output:
# Room Service

The vending machine hums its one dull note
all night, a monk devoted to nothing
but light and coins. I feed it dollars
I don't need to feed it, watch the coil
turn like a slow apology, releasing
what I didn't want, exactly—
salt, sugar, something to hold.

The sign hangs crooked on the door:
DO NOT DISTURB. As if a paper triangle
could keep out what already lives here,
unpacked in the closet, sleeping
in the shape of your coat.
I hung it anyway. Some griefs
require a doorknob, a small
brass permission to be still.

I ask the desk for a wake-up call
though I've been awake since April—
since the hospital's fluorescent hush,
since the nurse's hand and its terrible kindness.
Still, I like the idea of a stranger's voice
finding me in the dark, saying
*it's time*, as if time were a place
you could be delivered to,
gently, by name.

The ice machine down the hall
keeps its own hours, groaning
its cold into paper cups.
I go to it sometimes at 3 a.m.
not because I'm thirsty
but because the walk there and back
is a kind of proof: hallway, elevator light,
the small mechanics of still existing.

In the morning the maid will come
with her cart of clean sheets and small soaps,
and turn my sorrow into a made bed,
a folded towel shaped like a swan.
This is not nothing. This is the world
insisting: *rest here. someone
will remake this room for you again.*

I don't know where I'm going.
The lobby has fake flowers
that never die, which is its own
kind of promise. The wake-up call
will ring at seven. I will answer it
like a woman answering her own name,
surprised, each time,
to still be someone
who is called.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poem that contrasts the adjustable hospital bed with an ordinary hotel bed, exploring themes of illness, waiting, and relief.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bed That Remembers

The hotel bed does not care what you carry.
It holds you the way a stranger holds a door—
briefly, without question, then lets go.
You sink into a mattress bought
for average bodies, average nights,
sheets tucked with hospital corners
that have never met a hospital,
and you sleep like someone with nowhere
important to arrive.

The other bed hums.
It knows the language of elevation,
speaks in degrees—thirty for breathing,
forty-five for the fear of drowning
in your own lungs. Rails like ribs
that fold down when you're strong enough
to remember you have hands,
fold up when the night nurse decides
you might forget.

In the hospital bed, waiting is architecture.
You measure hours by shift changes,
by the particular squeak of the fourth wheel,
by how the light through the blinds
becomes a clock you didn't ask for.
The mattress remembers every position
of pain, adjusts itself to the shape
of your asking, though it cannot adjust
the thing that's actually wrong.

In the hotel bed, waiting is different—
you wait for morning like a gift,
not a verdict. The pillow doesn't know
your diagnosis. The remote controls
only the television, only
the temperature of a room
that isn't measuring your temperature too.

Relief, when it comes, arrives like this:
you are horizontal again, but chosen this time.
The bed beneath you asks nothing.
No numbers scroll above your head.
You are simply tired
the way vacation tires you,
not the way survival does.

You did not know a mattress could be innocent
until you'd slept in one that wasn't.
You did not know your body
could lie flat without apology
until some morning, weeks later,
you woke in an ordinary bed
and felt, for one entire breath,
nothing at all—

which is to say: everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
